channel.title: Acme: Science Fiction and Fantasy News
channel.description: Science fiction and fantasy fandom news, publishing, conventions, and history.

item.title: Weird Horror ends after 13 issues as Undertow plans to close the magazine site
item.description: Undertow Publications announced on November 7 that Weird Horror has published its final issue, with Locus reporting the closure on November 9. Issue 13, released in August 2026, ends a run that began in 2020 under editor Michael Kelly. The magazine published fiction, poetry, essays and interviews; two of its stories became World Fantasy Award finalists, and others reached year’s-best anthologies and Locus recommended lists. Undertow says the economics no longer work and plans to take the Weird Horror website offline in early 2027. Print and digital copies of all 13 issues remain available for now, giving readers and bibliographers a limited window to preserve the site’s material and document a notable small-press horror venue.

item.title: Goodreads opens 2026 Choice Awards voting across five genre-heavy categories
item.description: Goodreads opened the first round of its 18th annual Choice Awards on November 10. Registered members can vote through November 22 before finalists advance to a November 24–29 round; winners will be announced December 3. The ballot places 20 nominees in each of 15 categories, including Fantasy, Romantasy, Science Fiction, Horror, and Young Adult Fantasy and Science Fiction. Goodreads says eligibility covers English-language U.S. editions, including translations and major rereleases, published from November 12, 2025, through November 10, 2026. Because nominations derive from member activity and require a 3.50 average rating at launch, the slate offers a revealing snapshot of mass-reader taste rather than a juried genre award—a distinction likely to fuel discussion about visibility, category boundaries and popularity.

item.title: SFWA sets November 15 annual business meeting with member questions to follow
item.description: The Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association has scheduled its annual business meeting for Sunday, November 15, 2026, at 4 p.m. Pacific. SFWA says its board, staff and selected volunteers will review the organization’s year in advocacy, education and outreach, followed by a question-and-answer session. The online meeting is a useful institutional checkpoint after a year of publishing-contract disputes, censorship fights and continuing debate over professional support for genre writers. President Kate Ristau is listed as the featured participant. For fandom and publishing observers, the immediate date peg matters: the session arrives four days after this feed update and offers members a direct opportunity to hear how SFWA frames its priorities and to press leadership on unresolved concerns.
item.source: Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association

item.title: M. John Harrison becomes the first established science-fiction author to win the Booker
item.description: On November 9, M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, his post-apocalyptic 13th novel. At 81 he is the prize's oldest winner, and The Guardian identified him as the first author from the established science-fiction community to take the award. The judges, chaired by Mary Beard, reached a unanimous decision and awarded Harrison £50,000. The result caps six decades of formally adventurous work spanning the Viriconium stories, the Kefahuchi Tract novels and Climbers. For genre readers, the win is both a major late-career honor and a rare moment when a central figure in British speculative fiction is recognized by one of the English-language novel's most visible institutions.

item.title: STARLOG returns to print for its 50th anniversary
item.description: STARLOG's new annual print edition reaches newsstands on November 13, almost exactly 50 years after the magazine began in 1976. The 100-page Volume 2, Issue 1 is edited by science journalist and novelist Annalee Newitz, with original reporting, artwork and conversations about science fiction and real science. STARLOG was a crucial pre-web bridge among screen fandom, convention culture and behind-the-scenes production, particularly before specialized genre coverage became ubiquitous online. Fangoria's November 3 announcement provides the immediate date peg; the revived magazine itself is the anniversary object. The return should interest readers who remember Kerry O'Quinn's original run as well as historians tracking the periodic rebirth of once-dominant fan and professional media brands.

item.title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek's Captain Picard, dies at 86
item.description: Sir Patrick Stewart died at his Los Angeles home on October 28, his representative confirmed; CBS News updated its report on October 29. He was 86. Stewart brought Royal Shakespeare Company authority to Captain Jean-Luc Picard beginning with Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987, then carried the role through four films and three seasons of Star Trek: Picard. He also became widely known as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films while continuing a substantial stage career. His family's statement said he had experienced Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. The loss falls within this feed's 14-day window and marks the death of a performer whose Picard became one of modern science fiction's defining moral and intellectual figures.

item.title: Steve Davidson, who carried Amazing Stories into its second century, dies at 67
item.description: Amazing Stories announced on November 4, 2026, that publisher Steve Davidson died that day at age 67. Davidson acquired the historic magazine in 2012, rebuilt it first as a website and returned it to print through a 2018 Kickstarter. His death is a major new development in the story of a title founded by Hugo Gernsback in April 1926 as the first magazine devoted entirely to science fiction. The announcement credits Davidson with preserving that history while creating space for contemporary writers and fans. Kermit Woodall, who had taken over management when Davidson stepped back in 2022, says Amazing Stories will continue under his ownership and leadership during its centennial year.

item.title: FANAC digitizes a cross-section of 1950s through 2000s fan publishing
item.description: The Fanac Fan History Project's November 7, 2026 update added 17 scanned fanzine issues and one 1955 FAPA membership card. The batch ranges from Ectoplasm #1 (April 1951) and five issues of Ron Bennett's Burp! from 1954–55 to BCSFAzine #320 from January 2000. It also brings online three issues of H. P. Sanderson's Blunt, plus work edited by Rosemary Hickey, Elinor Busby, Lenny Bailes and others. The mix is useful institutional archaeology: clubzines, apazines and one-shot publications that are easily lost when collections remain private. FANAC says Joe Siclari supplied the scans unless otherwise noted, and the files are available through the linked update history.

item.title: The Man Who Fell to Earth returns to cinemas for its 50th anniversary
item.description: A timely 50th-anniversary restoration brings Nicolas Roeg's The Man Who Fell to Earth back to UK cinemas on November 13, 2026, followed by a five-disc collector's edition on November 16. The official October 6 announcement says the set includes the 4K film, Blu-ray, soundtrack, a 100-page booklet with a new Candy Clark interview and a 40-minute documentary, Bowie & Roeg: Aliens in America. Released in 1976 and adapted from Walter Tevis's novel, the film gave David Bowie his first major screen role as the stranded extraterrestrial Thomas Jerome Newton. The anniversary package also draws on archival interviews with Roeg and rarely seen production images, making it more substantial than a routine rerelease.

item.title: Edgar Rice Burroughs trilogy edition marks his 150th anniversary
item.description: On November 2, 2026, Subterranean Press opened a limited preorder window for ERB Books' three-volume edition of The Land That Time Forgot trilogy, explicitly issued for the 150th anniversary of Edgar Rice Burroughs' birth on September 1, 1875. The authorized set separates The Land That Time Forgot, The People That Time Forgot and Out of Time's Abyss into individual leather-bound hardbacks and adds more than 100 illustrations, including over 75 newly commissioned pieces. Contributors include Mark Schultz, William Stout, Bob Eggleton, Frank Frazetta, Roy Krenkel and J. Allen St. John. A portfolio of advertising pieces, notebook pages and correspondence makes the edition as much an exercise in pulp-history preservation as a luxury reprint.

item.title: eFanzines posts a substantial November batch of current fan publications
item.description: On November 2, 2026, eFanzines added seven new issues spanning several corners of print and digital fandom: Nic Farey's This Here... #105, Leigh Edmonds' The Chatter Box #35, Dale Speirs' Opuntia #641, Perry Middlemiss and David Grigg's Two Chairs in Print #20, Christopher J. Garcia's Claims Department #94, and two issues of Garcia's Hugo-winning The Drink Tank, #466 and #467. The update is a useful snapshot of fanzine culture as a continuing practice rather than only an archival subject. It also demonstrates the site's preservation role: eFanzines, founded December 8, 2000, maintains current publications beside deep collections of historic fan writing, convention reports and scanned Worldcon material.

item.title: New Star Trek visual history arrives on the original series' 60th anniversary
item.description: Ten Speed Press will publish Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History on November 10, 2026, during the franchise's 60th-anniversary year and exactly 60 years after “The Corbomite Maneuver” first aired on November 10, 1966. Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond's 416-page book covers the original series, the animated continuation and the first six feature films through 1991. Its archival material includes production photographs, costumes, storyboards, interviews, props, filming models and convention ephemera, alongside toys, comics and magazine covers. That breadth makes the volume potentially valuable to fan historians: it treats Star Trek not only as 79 television episodes and later films, but as a culture carried forward through conventions, collecting, publishing and licensed artifacts.

item.title: DAW acquires Julie E. Czerneda's Interstellar Diplomacy for the Underqualified
item.description: On November 5, 2026, DAW announced that it had acquired world rights to Julie E. Czerneda's Interstellar Diplomacy for the Underqualified. The publisher describes the novel as “cozy-ish” science fiction about a space-phobic scientist trapped aboard a starship who discovers that he may be the galaxy's best chance against a parasitic hive mind. DAW also frames it as a story about community and hope. The deal is notable because Czerneda, a biologist by training and a member of the Canadian Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame, has spent three decades building biologically informed far-future series including Species Imperative and The Clan Chronicles. The announcement gives established space-opera readers a fresh standalone premise while placing a veteran Canadian writer in DAW's current acquisition program.

item.title: Utopiales announces its 2026 juried prize winners
item.description: The Utopiales festival in Nantes, held October 29–November 1, 2026, has posted its 2026 prize list. Claire North's Les dieux lents, published in French by Le Bélial', received the Prix Utopiales, while Romain Benassaya's Cor Serpentis won the youth award and Cyril Bonin's Karl took the comics prize. The Prix Julia Verlanger went to R. J. Barker's Les Vaisseaux d'Os, and the festival's extraordinary prize recognized the French genre reference projects NooSFere and Quarante-deux. That last honor is especially resonant for fandom historians: both volunteer-driven resources preserve bibliographic, critical and community memory beyond the commercial life of individual books. The November 1 results offer an unusually broad snapshot of French-language speculative culture across prose, young readers, comics and fan-built scholarship.

item.title: Clarion West opens the road to its 2027 virtual workshop
item.description: Clarion West's October 16, 2026 announcement has a current November time peg: applications are opening for its 2027 virtual workshop, led by Premee Mohamed. The nine-month program will run from March through November 2027, extending the Seattle institution's recent experiment with a format designed around sustained writing, critique and professional development rather than six residential weeks. Clarion West also announced 2027 flash-fiction groups with Kij Johnson from June 3 through July 3 and said its six-week summer workshop will again be virtual. For fandom and publishing readers, this is more than a class listing. Clarion West has been a major pipeline and community institution since 1971, and its continued online structure shapes who can participate, how cohorts form, and what the workshop model may become.
